statement: A two-digit number is equal to 4 times the sum of its digits. When its two digits are swapped, the new number is 27 more than the original number. What is the original number?

choices.misconception: I used only the rule about the sum of the digits and took the first number that worked.
I used only the rule about swapping the digits and took the first number that worked, since 41 - 14 = 27.
I used only the rule about the sum of the digits and took the largest number that worked.
I found the right number but gave the number with its digits swapped instead of the original.

hints: Use one rule at a time to make a short list.
Write the number as 10a + b, with tens digit a and units digit b. The sum rule links a and b, leaving only a few candidates. Then work out how much swapping the digits changes each one.
The sum rule says 10a + b = 4a + 4b, so b = 2a: the candidates are 12, 24, 36 and 48. Swapping the digits of a number makes it bigger by 9 times the difference of its digits.

solutions.reliable: Call the digits a (tens) and b (units), so the number is 10a + b. The sum rule says 10a + b = 4(a + b), so 6a = 3b and b = 2a. That leaves 12, 24, 36 and 48. Now test the swap rule: 21 - 12 = 9, 42 - 24 = 18, 63 - 36 = 27, 84 - 48 = 36. Only 36 gives 27. Check: 4 × (3 + 6) = 36, and swapping gives 63, which is 27 more. The transferable idea: when a number must satisfy two conditions, use the easier one to make a short list, then test the list against the other.
solutions.elegant: Swapping the digits changes 10a + b into 10b + a, a change of 9(b - a). So the digits differ by 3, and the candidates are 14, 25, 36, 47, 58 and 69. Only 36 equals 4 times its digit sum.

whyOnTest: Digit-constraint puzzles with two rules test whether you write the number by place value and check every condition, not just the first one that gives a match.
